title: The Curse
objective: See what the curse does. Get ready to go east.

text.default:
You are crossing the market square when it happens.

A woman near the fountain stops walking. She does not slow down; she simply stops, between one step and the next, as though whatever was making her walk had run out and nothing had come to take its place. She stands with one foot a little in front of the other and her basket held in both hands, and her eyes are open and fixed on nothing at all.

Three people nearby see it. Two of them look away at once, as if they have had a good deal of practice at not seeing. The third, an older man, takes a step towards her and then stops himself.

You don't look away.
text.commander:
You go straight across to her. You don't run, because running draws attention, and attention won't help her.

Close to, she is completely still. She is breathing normally. When you step in front of her, her eyes follow you, very slightly. So she is in there, somewhere behind a face that has stopped.

"Can you hear me?" you say.
text.arcane:
You feel it before you see it. Something in the air tightens for a moment, as the pressure of the curse rises and then falls back, and then the woman stops.

You go to her and look at her carefully, letting your senses reach out. The curse lies thick on her. She has been months under it and nobody has done anything for her. This is not the beginning of it, you think. She is passing from one stage into the next.
text.ranger:
You move before you have quite understood why. You have been watching this town for three days, and you know at once that what has just happened to the woman is the thing everyone here is afraid of.

You go to her, as quietly as you would go up to anything that might bolt.
text.cipher:
You take in the square in the two seconds after it happens. Two people looked away; they have seen this before, and since they cannot mend it they have decided not to feel it. The older man stepped forward. He knows her.

You go to her, because whatever happens next will happen around her, and that is where you will learn something.

choices.text: Ask the old man her name, and try to reach her.

success.text:
The older man tells you her name, and you use it.

Something in her answers. She doesn't move or speak, but her attention seems to come a little nearer. You talk to her. You say her name twice more. You tell her that she is in the market square, that it is morning, and that her basket is heavy and she had better put it down.

She puts it down. Then she blinks, and looks at you in bewilderment, like somebody coming up out of cold water.

"I'm sorry," she says. She doesn't know what for.

success_at_cost.text:
You talk to her, and she doesn't quite come back. But after several minutes it passes of its own accord. She returns to herself by degrees, though not all the way, and looks at the basket in her hands as if surprised to find herself holding it.

At least you were there with her.

failure.text:
Nothing you say reaches her. In the end it passes of its own accord. She comes back to herself, looks at you with polite puzzlement, picks up her basket and walks on.

The older man watches her go. "Fifteen minutes this time," he says. "Last week it was thirty." He looks at you. "She doesn't remember them."

choices.text: Catch her before the basket pulls her over, and sit her on the fountain rim.

success.text:
You reach her just as her weight begins to go, with one hand on the basket and the other under her elbow. She is lighter than she looks. You sit her down on the rim of the fountain, and she stays where you put her.

The older man comes over then. "Ada," he says to her. "Ada, you're in the square." He says it to you as well, so that you will know her name.

After a while she looks at the basket in her lap and frowns at it, as though somebody else had packed it.

success_at_cost.text: You catch her, but not the basket, and turnips go rolling across the cobbles towards the dry fountain. You sit her on the rim. She doesn't notice the turnips. You pick them up one by one while she comes back.

failure.text: You are a step too slow. She goes down on one knee on the cobbles, and the basket with her. When she comes back she is on the ground without knowing why, and a stranger has hold of her elbow. She pulls her arm away.

success.text:
You step back and watch.

It goes on for some minutes. Nobody goes near her. The two who looked away have walked on, and the older man has decided against it. The market goes on round her as a stream goes round a stone.

Then, quite suddenly, she is back. She shifts the basket, glances at the fountain, and carries on to wherever she was going.

The older man catches your eye. "We've stopped making a fuss," he says. "It doesn't help, and they don't like being looked at."

success_at_cost.text: You watch. It passes, and she walks on. You have learned how long it lasts and how she comes out of it, but not much more.

failure.text: You watch, but the market is so used to this that there is nothing in it to see. Something has happened, and the town takes no notice.

default: In the hour after it happens you see all three powers in the town deal with it, and each of them shows you exactly what it is.

Two Compact soldiers turn up a few minutes after the woman has come round. They ask questions, quickly and without any warmth: how long it lasted, whether it has happened before, who her family are. They write it all down and go.

A Covenant priest arrives a little later. He speaks to the woman's neighbour rather than to the woman, and leaves a small packet of herbs with careful instructions. He doesn't charge for them. Nor does he say whether they will help.
A young man from the Rootless camp arrives last of all. He asks no questions. He sits with the woman for the best part of an hour and then helps her carry her basket home.

default.text: The Rootless man nods to you. He saw what you did.

text.commander:
You watch all three with a soldier's eye.

The Compact is collecting figures. The Covenant is easing the symptoms. The Rootless are doing what any decent person would do, which cannot be done for a whole town at once, and which is also the only thing that helps her today.

All three mean it, and none of the three is enough. The question is which of them you can work with.
text.arcane:
Each of the three tells you something of what that side really believes.

The Compact's questions are about patterns; they want figures from a great many cases. The Covenant's herbs come from an old tradition, which suggests they have read about the curse in books. The Rootless simply know what helps, from having done it, and nobody has written it down.

You would like to learn from all three. You doubt you can manage it without trouble.
text.ranger:
Each of them, in its way, is showing off its own method.

The Compact is orderly and thorough. The Covenant is sure of itself, and works from its book. The Rootless do whatever is in front of them.

You know which of those lasts in bad country. The Rootless have been here longest, and they are still here.
text.cipher:
Each of them, in its way, is showing off its own method.

But none of them is doing anything about the curse. They are only dealing with what it leaves behind. Somebody, sooner or later, is going to have to do more than that, and you would like to know who.

choices.text: Speak to the Compact soldiers before they leave.

success.text:
One of them, the older and more senior of the two, gives you a surprisingly straight answer.

"We're tracking how fast it gets worse," he says. "How long before the turns become permanent, and whether anything speeds it up or slows it down." He looks at his notes. "And before you ask, we don't know yet what we'll do with it. Commander Vorne's waiting till he's got enough to act on."

You wonder how much will be left of the town by the time he has enough.

success_at_cost.text: The younger soldier gives you the official line about monitoring and assessment and Commander Vorne's orders. You press him a little and he shuts up altogether.

failure.text: "Compact business, [sir/ma'am]," says the younger one. You are not Compact, so you get nothing.

choices.text: The older soldier says the lieutenant would like a word. Go to the gate.

default.text: "He was asking after you yesterday," the soldier says on the way. "He likes to know who's in town."

choices.text: The priest's boy says Edric would like a word. Go to the shrine.

default.text: The boy walks a step ahead of you the whole way and never once looks back to see whether you are following.

choices.text: Follow the Rootless man back towards the camp.

default.text:
He walks back through the trees like a man who does it often. When you catch him up he doesn't seem surprised.

"You were watching," he says.

"I wanted to understand what you were doing."

"Sitting," he says. "Just sitting." He thinks about it. "Maret says the worst of it is feeling alone in it. So we try not to leave them alone. Even if sitting doesn't mend anything."

He shrugs, as a man does who knows perfectly well it is not enough and means to go on doing it anyway.

choices.text: Move on. You've seen enough of Crestfall.

default.text: You have seen enough of the town and how it is coping. Whatever answer there is lies to the east. You begin to think about the road.

text.default:
It happens that evening in the Tallow, without any warning at all.

You are sitting at your usual table going over what you know, and you put a hand on the wall beside you without thinking, to steady yourself, and the wall is wrong.

It looks perfectly ordinary. But your hand feels something underneath it, a cold that isn't cold and a trembling that isn't movement, like a note being held somewhere too low to hear. It is in the wall, and in the building, and in the ground beneath the building.

For three or four seconds everything that is not the note seems rather less interesting.

Then it passes. You take your hand off the wall, and the room comes back as it was.
text.commander:
You sit still for a moment after it has passed. Soldiers learn to take note of anything strange their senses tell them, rather than jumping at it.

What you felt was everything outside you mattering less. It was not unpleasant, and that is what you must remember. It would be very easy to touch the wall again.

You don't touch the wall again.
text.arcane:
You sit with your hand in the air and go over what you have just felt, carefully, as you were trained to.

The curse is in the fabric of the town. It is not in the air but in the ground and the stone, in the very stuff of a place that has stood near it so long that the line between inside and outside has worn away.

You write: first direct contact with the curse at work. Three or four seconds. Attention narrowed. Not painful. It is a good deal easier now to see why people do not fight it.
text.ranger:
Something reached you through the wall, and you know it at once.

You have moved away from the wall before you have decided to. You sit in the middle of the room and find that the middle feels different from the edges. The edges are where the building meets the ground, and the ground is where the thing is.

You stop touching walls.
text.cipher:
You write it down as plainly as you can.

It lasted three or four seconds. Everything outside it seemed to matter less. It did not hurt, and it did not frighten you, and that is what matters. You can see how it becomes a habit. Somebody with a hard life in a hard place might go back to it again and again, until going back was all they did.

You don't touch the wall again.

default.text:
He listens, and doesn't look surprised.

"The building's stood here sixty years," he says. "The ground's been soaking for three." He wipes the bar. "Keeps mostly to the edges. I moved the tables into the middle two years back."

He looks at the wall. "Wren, the man by the fire, used to touch the wall by his chair three times a day. Did it for a year before I moved the chair. I thought it was habit." He pauses. "Well. It was habit."

choices.text: Keep it to yourself, and write it down.

default.text:
You write it down: the date, the hour, how long it lasted and what it was like. You set it down as plainly as a weather report and close the book.

Then you move your chair into the middle of the room.

choices.text: Put your hand back on the wall, and listen.

success.text:
You put your palm flat against the plaster and wait.

It is there again, under the wall and under the floor. It is not a sound but a pressure, very low, that rises and falls a little like breathing. And it comes from the east.

You take your hand away before it can have any more of your attention. The room is a little quieter than it was.

success_at_cost.text: You find the note again, and it finds you, and this time it keeps you longer. When you take your hand away the fire has burned low and Aldous is looking at you from the bar. He doesn't ask.

failure.text: You put your hand back on the wall and the note comes up your arm all at once. Everything else goes thin: the fire, the room, the reason you came. When it lets go you are sitting with your hand in your lap, and you can't remember putting it there.

text.default:
The night goes by. You sit with what you know and what you don't, and you make a list.

You know that [missing person] was here fourteen months ago, went east, and left a letter with Maret. You know the curse is real, because you have felt it. You know it comes from the ruins, and that three different parties each want something from them. And you know Maret has an arrangement she won't altogether explain.

You don't know what is in the ruins, or what became of [missing person], or whether the letter they left was a warning or an invitation or both.

Tomorrow you take the east road.
text.commander:
You go through it as you would before any operation: what you know, what you don't, what you have, and what may go wrong.

You know the direction, the destination, and roughly how long ago they went, and you know what each of the three sides is after. You don't know what is in the ruins or where [missing person] is now. You have your pay, your training, and two half-made arrangements with two of the three sides. As for what may go wrong, there is the curse, and the forest, and three parties pulling different ways, and the danger of caring too much how it turns out.

That last you have no way of measuring.
text.arcane:
You write one more entry before the lamp goes out.

The pressure I have felt since I came to Ashenveld is strongest towards the east. It fits a single source that does not move and spreads outward from where it is. The ruins.

The curse does not mean any harm, as a person might. It is there, and its being there has consequences. The question is not what it wants. The question is what one does about a thing that wants nothing at all and is destroying everything regardless.

I mean to find out.
text.ranger:
You go through your pack in the dark, by feel. Everything is there, and you need all of it.

The east road won't be like the roads you know. It isn't only weather and animals you will have to watch for there. Whatever is in the ruins has changed the land itself, and you will have to learn to read it all over again.

You have done that before, and you will manage.
text.cipher:
You go over it once more before you sleep.

Maret, Aldous, Edric and Corvin all know things, and each of them has given you something and kept something back. Cael and Edric want something from you, and very possibly Maret does too. And the ones who may matter most are Lira, and Branch, and the old woman in the market whose daughter the camp fed.

As for [missing person], they went east fourteen months ago, and they were smiling when they went in.

And tomorrow you go east yourself.

choices.text: Walk round the Compact's perimeter after curfew, and count what they're guarding.

success.text:
After curfew you walk the long way round the granary, as you have walked a hundred perimeters, and count.

There are two sentries where one would do. There is fresh straw in the stables, enough for twenty horses, and in the yard there are new bunks still in their timber, stacked and waiting. They are not guarding what they have. They are making room for what is coming.

Thirty men, you would guess, and somebody senior enough to want a room to himself.

success_at_cost.text: You get most of the way round before a sentry's lamp swings your way. You have seen enough, though: new bunks stacked in the yard, and more beds than there are soldiers. Somebody is coming.

failure.text: A sentry calls out before you are halfway round. You give him a name that is not yours and go back to the Tallow, and lie awake wondering what you missed.

choices.text: Put your palm flat on the inn wall and listen properly.

success.text:
You wait until the room is empty, then put your palm flat on the plaster and stop holding yourself apart from it.

The note comes from the east, a little to the south. It has a pulse to it, very slow, like something breathing in its sleep. It runs under the inn and the town and the road, all the way to the forest.

You take your hand away and write it down before you can lose it.

success_at_cost.text: You find the note, and the pulse in it, and then it finds you back. When you take your hand away the candle has burned down a full inch.

failure.text: The note is there, but it won't keep still for you. You give it up before it costs you more than a night's sleep.

choices.text: Go to the east gate at midnight and read the road.

success.text:
The soldiers on the gate are watching the town, not the road. You crouch in the mud just beyond the reach of their lamp and read it.

A great many people have gone east on foot, barefoot and close together, with the short even stride of people neither hurrying nor stopping. One set of tracks comes back, booted, months old and pressed deep. Somebody walked out to the far end of this road and came back carrying something heavy.

You know the road now. It won't surprise you tomorrow.

success_at_cost.text: You read enough before the cold drives you in. A great many bare feet have gone east, and almost nothing has come back.

failure.text: It rained in the afternoon and the road has nothing to tell you. You go back to bed with wet knees.

choices.text: Think over what Maret didn't say.

success.text:
You go back over everything Maret said to you, and this time you listen for the tense.

Not once did she say they were. Whenever she spoke of [missing person], she said they are. They know the ruins. They are careful. They are not the sort to.

Maret believes they are alive. She has believed it for fourteen months and told nobody, because then she would have to explain why she has not gone in after them.

success_at_cost.text: There was something in the way Maret spoke of them that has stayed with you. You turn it over half the night without being able to put a name to it. You only know that it was hopeful, and that she would hate you for noticing.

failure.text: You go over it all again and again, and end up exactly where you started, with less sleep.

choices.text: Sleep, and take the east road in the morning.

default.text: You put out the lamp and make yourself sleep. You will need it tomorrow.
